title: Edge-Orientation Entropy Predicts Preference for Diverse Types of Man-Made Images
research_question: To investigate whether edge-orientation entropy is associated with aesthetic preference in a wide variety of man-made visual patterns and scenes, and whether edge-orientation entropy relates to the human preference for curved over angular shapes, including whether these properties share predicted variance for visual stimuli.

participants.description: University students or graduates, younger than 40 years, normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Specific Ns for each experiment: Exp 1: 20; Exp 2: 31 (mean 25.8 years, 12 male); Exp 3: 27 (mean 26.4 years, 14 male); Exp 4: 18; Exp 5: 27 (same as Exp 3); Exp 6: 31 (same as Exp 2).
participants.recruitment: Advertisements in places frequented by students of various disciplines

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Simple irregular geometric shapes with a black contour on a white background, consisting of either curved or straight lines (180 combinations).
Artificial ornamental patterns generated with Taprats software, 500x500 pixels.
Photographs of building facades (Vienna and Berlin), 500x500 pixels, luminance histograms equalized.
Color images of interior architectural scenes, varying in curvilinearity, ceiling height, and openness.
Music album covers from three genres: pop, metal, and classic music.
Complex artificial line patterns composed of 40 either angular or curved line elements, systematically varied in 2nd-order edge-orientation entropy.

measures.instrument: Continuous-looking free scale (0-100 steps, converted to 0-1)
Shannon entropy of summary orientation histogram (24 Gabor filter bins)
Shannon entropy of pairwise edge orientation comparisons (distance-dependent)
PHOG descriptor-derived measure (mean value for pyramid levels 1-3)
Binary variables (ceiling height: high/low; openness: open/closed)

mechanisms: Humans prefer high edge-orientation entropy because it indicates a more uniform distribution of edge orientations, which may be related to processing fluency or reduced prediction error.
The preference for curved shapes over angular shapes is a robust phenomenon, possibly linked to angularity reflecting potential danger or threat.
Edge-orientation entropy and curvilinearity share a large portion of predicted variance for aesthetic preference, suggesting they might operationalize similar visual properties.
Self-similarity and edge density also contribute to aesthetic ratings, with their effects varying depending on the specific aesthetic judgment (pleasing, interesting, harmonious) and image category.

The effect of image properties on aesthetic ratings is stronger for abstract stimuli or those evaluated predominantly based on visual structure, compared to images with recognizable content where content-based biases may diminish the effect of formal properties.
moderators: Type of images analyzed (simple shapes, ornamental patterns, building facades, interior scenes, music album covers, complex line patterns)
Range of entropy values encountered in the stimuli
Type of aesthetic rating (pleasing, interesting, harmonious, preference, pleasantness, beauty)
Architectural features (openness, ceiling height, contour for interior scenes)
implementation_implications: Designers and architects could consider edge-orientation entropy as an objective measure to predict aesthetic preference in man-made environments.
For abstract patterns and architectural facades, manipulating edge-orientation entropy can significantly influence how pleasing or interesting they are perceived.

The findings suggest that the preference for curvilinearity might be partly operationalized by edge-orientation entropy, offering a more mathematically precise way to quantify this aspect of visual form.

limitations: Findings are specific to the laboratory setting and may not generalize to real-world environments.
Analysis was restricted to six special types of man-made images, and findings may not generalize to other man-made or natural patterns/scenes.
Aesthetic ratings can be domain-specific, and the study did not cover a wide range of domains.
Participants were undergraduates or recent graduates, all younger than 40 years, which may limit generalizability due to idiosyncratic taste or cultural content.
The study focused on group-level differences and did not address inter-individual variability in aesthetic ratings.
